results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long to keep tax records**

| Record type | Minimum retention period | Notes & Source |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------|
| **General income‑and‑deduction records** | **3 years** after the return is filed (or 4 years if a later extension was filed) – unless a longer period applies | *Records that support an item of income or deduction must be kept until the limitation period for that return expires* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Missing or underreported income that is >25 % of the return** | **6 years** | *Table 3 in Segment 1 shows a 6‑year limit for omitted income above 25 % of gross* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Fraudulent or false returns** | **No limit** (indefinitely) | *Table 3 states “Not limited” for fraudulent returns* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Employment tax records** (e.g., payroll, Forms 941, 940, 944, W‑2s, 1099s) | **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later | *“If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Records related to property (assets)** | Until the limitation period expires for the year you dispose of the property | *“Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Copies of filed tax returns** | **At least** the same period as the supporting records (i.e., the longest limitation period that applies) | *“Keep copies of your filed tax returns”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |
| **Other records that may be needed for non‑tax purposes** | Until you determine an additional requirement (e.g., insurance, creditors) | *“When your records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you check to see if you have to keep them longer for other purposes”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16). |

### How to determine which “limit” applies

1. **Determine the “period of limitations” for the return** – this is the time you have to amend your return or the IRS has to assess additional tax.  
   *Typical periods:* 3 years for most cases; 6 years if income omitted >25 %; no period for fraud.  
2. **Add any additional tax‑specific retention rules** (e.g., 4 years for employment taxes).  
3. **For assets, keep records until you sell or otherwise dispose of them in a taxable transaction, and then keep those records until the end of the limitation period for that disposal year.**

### Bottom line

- Hold all income‑supporting documents for **3 years** (or **6 years** if you omitted >25 % of income, or **indefinitely** if the return was fraudulent).  
- Keep **employment tax records for 4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid.  
- Keep **asset records until the limitation period expires after you dispose of the asset**.  
- Never discard records before confirming that no other agency (e.g., insurance, creditors) requires a longer retention period.

These durations satisfy the IRS’s requirements for records needed for **administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You must keep business records because they are the evidence that the IRS and other agencies need to determine the correctness of your tax returns, to monitor your business’s financial health, and to satisfy various legal and regulatory obligations.

- **Support your tax returns** – Every figure you report on a tax return must be backed by documentation. The IRS can test your electronic record‑keeping system (or paper records) to verify that you reported income and deductions correctly. Without those records you cannot prove that the amounts on your return are accurate or defend yourself in an audit.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- **Document the source of income and expenses** – Receipts, invoices, purchase orders, bank deposits, checkbooks, and other supporting documents show where money came from and how it was spent. This helps you distinguish business from personal receipts, separate taxable from nontaxable income, and identify deductible expenses.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- **Prepare future tax returns and financial statements** – Consistent, organized records give you the data you need for future returns, for preparing profit‑and‑loss statements, balance sheets, and for reporting to creditors or investors.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Compliance with legal and employment requirements** – Many industries (e.g., with payroll or safety records) require documentation to demonstrate compliance with labor laws, safety regulations, and insurance filings.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- **Retention for the period of limitations** – The IRS must be able to review your records for as long as the statute of limitations allows for any claim or assessment (usually 3–6 years, or longer for employment tax and depreciation matters).  You should keep records at least until that period expires, and possibly longer if other agencies (e.g., creditors, insurers) require them.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

In short, keeping thorough, accurate records is essential for:  
1. Supporting every item on your tax return,  
2. Protecting yourself against audits and penalties,  
3. Managing and improving your business, and  
4. Fulfilling legal, employment, and regulatory obligations.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**

2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
**Which accounting method should you use?** Your tax‑reporting method is chosen the first time you file a business income return (a Schedule C with Form 1040). After that you stay with that method unless you obtain IRS approval to change it. | Method | How you record income | How you record expenses | Typical users | What you need to keep in mind | |--------|-----------------------|------------------------|--------------|-------------------------------| | **Cash method** | Income is counted when you actually receive or are constructively *received* that money. | Expenses are deducted in the year you actually *pay* them. | Most single‑member sole‑prop owners, freelancers, and small owners without inventory or with very small inventory. | • If you have inventory, you usually **must** use accrual for sales and purchases, unless you qualify as a *small business taxpayer* who can treat inventory as non‑incidental material.
• You must keep separate books showing when you receive money and when you pay money.
• Changing from cash to another method requires filing Form 3115. |  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | | **Accrual method** | Income is counted when you earn it (the event of earning has occurred and you can estimate a reasonable amount), even if you haven’t received the cash yet. | Expenses are deducted (or capitalized) when you incur them, regardless of when you pay. | Businesses that keep inventory, sell on credit, or need to match income and expenses more accurately. | • Requires tracking accounts receivable and payable.
• Requires an *inventory* calculation each year (unless you’re a small‑business taxpayer that can treat inventory as non‑incidental).
• You must use the same accrual approach for all income and expenses; mixing cash for some items and accrual for others is allowed only if you keep clear records and the mix still shows income consistently.
• Changing from accrual to another method also needs Form 3115. |  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | | **Special or combination methods** | You can blend any of the above (cash, accrual, and special methods like depreciation, amortization, etc.) as long as the overall approach *clearly shows your income* and you keep consistent books. | You must use the same method for all related income and expenses.
Inventory rules still apply: if inventory is needed you must use accrual for sales/purchases, but you may use cash for other items. | Small businesses that need a hybrid approach (e.g., cash for routine expenses but accrual for sales that require inventory). | • If you use a combination that includes the cash method, treat the whole combination as cash.
• Changing to a different mix still requires approval via Form 3115. |  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | ### How to decide 1. **Do you keep inventory?** * If **yes**, you’re normally required to use the accrual method for sales and purchases, unless you qualify as a *small business taxpayer* (average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million) and choose to treat inventory as *non‑incidental materials* or *supplies* (you deduct them when first used). See [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) for details on the inventory exception. 2. **Are you a small business taxpayer?** * If your average annual receipts for the past 3 years are ≤ $31 million (inflation‑adjusted) and you’re not a tax shelter, you qualify to use the cash method even if you keep inventory. See [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). 3. **Do you prefer simplicity?** * The cash method is simpler: you record revenue when you actually get the cash and expenses when you actually pay. It’s often recommended for sole proprietors, freelancers, and service businesses that don’t handle inventory.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 4. **Do you need to match income and expenses more closely?** * The accrual method gives a better match between income earned and expenses incurred, which is useful if you have credit sales or inventory shrinkage.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 5. **Will you change your method later?** * Any change after the first tax return must be approved by the IRS by filing Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method); you may have to pay a user fee.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) ### Quick decision guide | Question | Likely choice | |----------|---------------| | **Do you sell goods you keep on hand?** | Use accrual (unless you meet the small‑business inventory exception). | | **Do you only provide services and nothing is held in inventory?** | Cash method is usually fine. | | **Do you want the simplest bookkeeping and have modest receipts?** | Cash method. | | **Do you want the most accurate picture of when you earned money versus when you spent it?** | Accrual method. | --- **Bottom line:** - **Cash** if you have no inventory or qualify for the small‑business inventory exception. - **Accrual** for most businesses that keep inventory or want precise matching of income and expenses. - **Combination** if you need both approaches, but remember it still needs to “clearly show your income” and may require IRS approval to change. Once you pick, keep your books consistent, and remember that a later change requires Form 3115.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) **Sources:** 1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) 2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) 4. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 17)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the steps and tools described in the handbook:

1. **Conduct routine self‑inspections**  
   * Identify hazards and control them.  
   * Monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify they stay effective.  
   * Use qualified workers for the inspection.  
   * If needed, get free help from an OSHA On‑Site Consultation program.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists**  
   * Pick the checklists that match the most critical areas of your business.  
   * Update or delete items so they match your actual work processes.  
   * At the end of each checklist you’ll find links to additional resources on that topic.  
   * Remember: the checklists are for identifying hazards, not for checking compliance with OSHA laws.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Compile and analyze the data**  
   * Combine checklist results with injury&illness records, worker training data, maintenance logs, and incident reports.  
   * Use this combined information to see where the biggest problems lie.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Take action and keep records**  
   * Implement controls (engineering, administrative, personal protective equipment).  
   * Record what controls you added and when workers were trained about them.  
   * Review the program with workers and update it when things change.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

5. **Use OSHA and NIOSH resources**  
   * Check the OSHA website for regulations that apply to your workers, machines, and materials.  
   * Use OSHA videos, quick‑takes, and the Safety and Health Topics pages for guidance.  
   * If you need help figuring out which standards apply, call the national OSHA hotline (1‑800‑321‑OSHA).  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

6. **Keep the process continuous**  
   * Perform inspections regularly (e.g., after significant changes to the workplace).  
   * Repeat the data‑collection, analysis, and control‑implementation cycle to keep hazards in check.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

By following these steps—self‑inspection, checklist use, data compilation, action, and ongoing review—you’ll systematically uncover and manage workplace hazards.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)
3. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 9)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. Accrual Accounting – What’s Different?** | Feature | Cash Method | Accrual Method | |---------|-------------|----------------| | **When income is reported** | In the tax year you actually receive (or constructively receive) the money.
For example, a check received on December 30, 2024 but deposited on January 4, 2025 is included in 2025 income because it was constructively received in 2025. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | In the year the income is earned, even if the money is received later. You include it when “all events that fix the right to receive the income have occurred” and the amount can be reliably determined. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | | **When expenses are deducted** | In the year you actually pay the expense (or, if paid in advance, only the portion that applies to that tax year).
Example: A $1,000 insurance policy for July 1 – June 30 is split 50/50 between the two years. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | In the year the expense is incurred—when liability is fixed and the cost is reasonably determinable. This matches expenses to the income they helped generate. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | | **Inventory treatment** | Generally allowed only if you have no inventory. If inventory is carried, you must still use accrual for purchases and sales because you need to match revenue to cost. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | If you keep inventory, you must use accrual for purchases and sales; inventory must be valued at the start and end of the year to compute cost of goods sold. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | | **Constructive receipt** | You must include income when it is available to you without restriction (e.g., a deposit in a bank account). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | Same test applies for accrual, but income is included in the year earned, not necessarily when it becomes available. | | **Example of timing difference** | If you buy office supplies in December 2025, receive a bill in December, but pay in January 2026, you can still deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed. (Cash method would allow deduction only when paid.) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | • Example: Sell a computer on December 28, 2025, billed in January 2026, paid February 2026. You must include the income in 2025 because you earned it in that year. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | **Why the difference matters** - **Cash method** is simpler and often used by small businesses with no inventory, because you only track actual cash flows. - **Accrual method** matches income and expenses to the same period, giving a truer picture of profitability, especially when you have inventory or credit sales. **Bottom line** Cash accounting records money when it changes hands; accrual accounting records the economic event—when you earn or incur something—regardless of when cash moves. **Sources:** 1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) 2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) 3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) 4. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes. The IRS allows a self‑employed person or sole proprietor to deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while traveling away from one’s tax home for business purposes. The deductions cover the main categories of travel costs and have some specific rules and limits. **1. Definition of a deductible business trip** You are traveling “away from home” when * your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home for longer than a normal workday, **and** * you need sleep or rest to be able to perform your work while away. These are the two conditions that make travel expenses deductible【Segment 2】. **2. What can be deducted** | Category | What can be taken as a deduction (and limits) | Source | |----------|----------------------------------------------|--------| | **Transportation to and from business destination** | Airfare, train, bus, or car travel between home and the business location, plus taxi, commuter‑bus, or limousine fared between airport/rail‑station, hotel, or work site. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | | **Car or truck use** | • Business portion of a rented vehicle or a vehicle you own or lease.
• You may use either the actual‑expense method (fuel, gas, oil, insurance, parking, tolls, repairs, …) or the standard mileage rate (in 2025, 70 ¢ per mile). See Pub. 463 for full limits. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Other incidental expenses** | Baggage handling or shipping of samples or display materials, telephone or fax calls made while traveling, tips paid, and dry‑cleaning/laundry for the trip. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | | **Employee reimbursements** | The amount you reimburse employees for travel and meal expenses is deductible as a business expense if you reimburse under an accountable or non‑accountable plan (the rules are in Pub. 15). | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) | **3. results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
The executive summary is the first part of a business plan and is meant to give a concise overview of the entire proposal. According to the provided material, it should be brief—usually one or two paragraphs—and include:

* A description of the business idea  
* The amount of funding needed and how it will be used  
* The amount of money the owner has already invested (or will invest)  
* A short timeline or schedule of major goals and milestones  
* (It is usually written last, after the rest of the plan is complete)  

These elements are designed to let a reader quickly understand the purpose, financial needs, and projected progress of the business.

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the guidance in the business‑plan outline:

1. **Define the niche** – Identify the best customer for your product or service.  
2. **Describe characteristics** – Include demographics (age, gender, income), geography, lifestyle, product use, or benefits sought.  
3. **Segment** – For business markets, segment by industry, company size, location, or use/application; for consumer markets, segment by demographics, geography, economic status, lifestyle, or benefits sought.  
4. **Estimate size and growth** – Use population figures, industry reports, or sales data to estimate the approximate size of the target market and its growth potential.  
5. **Project capture** – Estimate what share of the total market you expect to capture.  

These steps give a clear, data‑driven description of your target market. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  Because your shop serves the public, it is a **public accommodation** under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).  All public‐accommodation businesses must remove barriers that are *readily achievable* and must provide an accessible route, entrance, and places where goods or services are sold or delivered.  Existing facilities that were built before the ADA do not receive a blanket exemption; they must still comply to the extent that removal is readily achievable [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

**What that means for your shop**

| What you must provide | Minimum requirements (ADA standards) | Key segment citations |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **Accessible route** – a continuous path that can be used by a person in a wheelchair –    | Minimum 30 inches wide, at least 36 inches where a turn or a turn‑stile is required (36 inches long, 36 inches high for a door, 32 inches opening for a turnstile) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Accessible entrance** – the first point of entry to the building | Door opening at least 36 inches wide (or 32 inches clear width when fully opened), door hardware that can be operated without a tight grasp, ramp slope no steeper than 1:12, handrails if vertical rise > 6 in | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Accessible sales or service counter** | Counter face at least 36 inches long, no higher than 36 inches above the floor; 30 in × 48 in clear floor space in front of it | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Accessible portion of the store floor** – aisles and shelving | Aisles at least 36 inches wide, 3 ft × 3 ft turning space at corners, 60 in × 60 in space for a 180‑degree turn | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Signage to an accessible entrance** | Clear arrows or the International Symbol of Accessibility; posted on an accessible route and ≤ 48 inches high | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible parking** (if you have a lot) | One accessible space for < 25 spaces (eight‑foot wide access aisle), or as required by local rules; if you have a van‑accessible space, it must be a car space as well | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Alternative services** | If any of the above cannot be achieved “readily,” you must provide a service that lets the customer use the store (e.g., assistance with retrieving items, home delivery, or in‑store pickup at an accessible location) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |

**How to determine “readily achievable”**  
A barrier is *readily achievable* if it can be removed or changed without **significant difficulty or expense** relative to the business size and resources.  Larger businesses are expected to take a more active role; smaller businesses have fewer resources but still must do what is feasible.  If a barrier is **not** readily achievable, you may postpone the change, but you must provide an alternative service for that part of the store so people with disabilities can still use it [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).

**Bottom line**  
You are required by the ADA to make your shop wheelchair accessible to the extent that removing barriers is readily achievable.  The standards give specific minimum widths, heights, and signage requirements, and if any part cannot be fixed easily, you must provide a reasonable alternative method for disabled customers to access goods or services.  Failure to comply can result in enforcement actions and legal liability.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You’re not automatically exempt—only specific employers qualify for limited exemption from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping.

- **Partial exemption** applies if **(1)** you had 10 or fewer employees during every calendar year in the last year **or** **(2)** your business is in one of the low‑hazard industries listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  In those cases, you can avoid keeping the OSHA Form 300, 301, and 300A logs.  However, you must still report **all work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA.  These reporting requirements apply to all employers, irrespective of size or industry.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**  
(Information only from the provided documents)

---

### 1. Decide what type of business you will operate  
* Sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, C‑corp, or S‑corp – each has different tax rules and filing requirements. See the “What New Business Owners Need To Know” section and “Determining Which Type of Business to Use.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

### 2. Get the required identification numbers  
* **EIN (Employer Identification Number)** – needed for most businesses, even if you have no employees. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
* If you have employees, you also need the **payee’s identification number** for withholding. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

### 3. Choose a tax year and accounting method  
| → Date you first file your return (or change) | Action needed | Form | Deadline * |
|------------------------------------------------|---------------|------|-----------|
| 1. **Tax year** – calendar year (Jan 1‑Dec 31) or fiscal year (any other 12‑month period) | File first return with the chosen year. For a change, file **Form 1128** and may need a fee. | 1128 | “The date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.” – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| 2. **Accounting method** – cash or accrual (or special) | Pick the method on the first return. Change later requires IRS approval (Form 3115). | 3115 | – [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |

*Cash method* records income when received and expenses when paid.  
*Accrual method* records income when earned and expenses when incurred.  
If you keep inventory, the accrual method is usually required. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

### 4. Set up a bookkeeping system  
* Keep separate books for each business if you operate more than one. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
* Use journals, ledgers, and a **business checkbook** as the main source of entries. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
* Track **gross receipts** (cash register tapes, bank deposits, receipts books) and **supporting documents** (invoices, canceled checks, deposit slips). [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
* If you keep records electronically, the system must index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce them in legible form. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

### 5. Record every business transaction  
* Sales, purchases, payroll, expenses, and asset acquisitions/disposals must be logged.  
* Use **petty‑cash slips** for small cash payments. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
* For assets, keep purchase invoices, closing statements, and records of depreciation, section 179 deductions, and gains/losses. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

### 6. Keep your records for the required time  
| Type of record | Minimum retention period | Source |
|----------------|--------------------------|--------|
| General business records that support income or deductions | Until the period of limitations expires (usually 3‑7 years) | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment tax records | 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset records (depreciation, etc.) | Until the period of limitations for the year you dispose of the asset | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

### 7. Understand your tax obligations and filing schedule  
| Tax / Form | Who files | When it’s due |
|------------|-----------|---------------|
| **Income tax** – Schedule C (or F) with Form 1040 or 1040‑SR | Sole proprietors, partners, S‑corp shareholders | 15th day of 4th month after year‑end (e.g., 15 Apr) | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Self‑employment tax** – Schedule SE with Form 1040 | Sole proprietors, partners, S‑corp shareholders | Same as income tax | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| **Estimated tax** – Form 1040‑ES | Anyone who expects ≥ $1 000 (or $500 for C‑corp) of tax | 15th of 4th, 6th, 9th, and 1st month after year‑end | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Employment taxes** – Forms 941 (quarterly) or 944 (annual) | Employers with employees | 30 Apr, 31 Jul, 31 Oct, 31 Jan (or 30 Apr for 944) | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Federal unemployment (FUTA)** – Form 940 | Employers | 31 Jan, 30 Apr

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe **and** make the premises accessible, your workplace should meet the basic requirements laid out in the Small‑Business Safety and Health Handbook. The handbook is organized around a safety program plus specific accessibility provisions.  

---

### 1.  Establish a Safety & Health Program  
* **Management leadership & worker participation** – The program must be owned by management but must also involve employees in identifying hazards. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
* **Hazard identification & control** – Regular inspections (e.g., for spills, obstructions, loose flooring) should be scheduled and documented. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)  
* **Education & training** – Provide OSHA‑approved training (e.g., 10‑hour outreach) for all workers and specialty training on site‑specific hazards. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=88)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=89)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=92)  
* **Program evaluation & improvement** – Review the program annually and update it when conditions change. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
* **Emergency action plan** – Include evacuation routes, assembly points, assistance for people with disabilities, and communication methods.  The plan should designate who orders evacuations and how visitors are assisted. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)  

---

### 2.  Keep the Workplace Free of Hazards  

| Hazard area | Key requirement | Segment |
|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| **Walkways & Working Surfaces** | Keep clear, dry, and free of tripping hazards; implement non‑slip mats where wet. Provide guardrails where surfaces >4 ft high. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) |
| **Re–shoring & Fall Protection** | Guardrails or fall‑protection systems for elevated surfaces. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) |
| **Machinery & Equipment** | Lock‑out/tag‑out, clear labeling of emergency stop, and proper guarding of moving parts. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=53)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) |
| **Electrical** | Adequate clearance, use non‑conductive ladders in wet areas, lock out energized circuits. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=17) |

---

### 3.  Provide an Accessible Entrance and Pathways  

| Feature | Minimum requirement | Segment |
|---------|--------------------|---------|
| **Ramp** | Slope not steeper than 1:12; handrails on both sides for rises >6 in; width ≥36 in; landing ball‑park 18 in wide. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Door** | Minimum 36‑in clearance; use lever handle or loop handle instead of round knob/short‑handle; width ≥36 in. | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Signage** | If a second entrance is used, sign must direct to the accessible entrance. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Tactile & Audible** | Where applicable, provide tactile indicators for blind workers. | (not explicitly in provided segments – therefore not covered) |

---

### 4.  Accessible Parking & Transit  

* **Parking** – Each space must have an access aisle: 8‑ft wide for vans, 5‑ft wide for cars; clear vertical height ≥98 in; symbol of accessibility mounted high. Doors to the parcel must be marked “VA‑ACCESSIBLE” for van spaces. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Route** – The path from the parking area to the entrance must be level, slip‑resistant, and free of steps or steep slopes. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |

---

### 5.  Accessible Work Stations & Services  

* **Counters** – Accessible counter height ≤36 in and at least 36 in long; a 30 in × 48 in clear space in front for wheelchair access. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
* **Sales & Assistance** – If an accessible counter cannot be installed, provide a modular or auxiliary counter, or use a mobile board. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |

---

### 6.  Exits and Fire Safety  

* **At least two egress routes** from each level; each exit marked with illuminated “EXIT” signs (≥6 in high, ≥¾ in wide). | [[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |
* **Emergency lighting** – Test every 30 s each month and 90 min annually. | [[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |

---

### 7.  Additional Practical Tips  

* Keep walkways and aisles wide enough for wheelchair maneuvering (minimum 36 in, 3–4 ft recommended if traffic is heavy). | [[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
* Repair or cover holes in flooring and sidewalks immediately. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) |
* Use locks or alarms so that accessible doors can be opened by staff without security concerns. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |

---

**Summary**  
Set up a clear safety and health program that includes training, regular inspections, and an emergency plan. Keep walkways and surfaces well‑maintained, guard machinery, and ensure all electrical work follows safe‑clearance rules. Make sure at least one entrance, a ramp or doorway, and an exit are fully compliant with ADA accessibility standards. Provide accessible parking, ramps, and sales counters, and ensure the building’s egress routes are visible, illuminated, and free of obstruction.

*This answer draws only on the information in the supplied segments.*

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Cover Page** – include company name, address, phone, owners, date, logo if any [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
2. **Table of Contents** (optional) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
3. **Executive Summary** – a brief one‑to‑two‑paragraph overview of the idea, required capital, use of funds, and a short schedule of goals [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
4. **Business Description** – describe the product/service, sustainable competitive advantage, relevant regulations, facilities, and equipment [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
5. **Management Plan** – outline the organizational structure, key roles, responsibilities, and the qualifications of managers and owners [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).  
6. **Market Analysis** – detail total market size, target market, competitors, and marketing strategy [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
7. **Financial “Money” Section** – include:  
   * **Sources and Uses of Funds** – list assets (land, building, equipment, inventory, working capital) and financing (equity, loans) so the two totals match [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=21).  
   * **Three‑Year Income Projection** – monthly projections for revenue and expenses [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  
   * **Cash‑Flow Statement** – projected cash inflows and outflows for three years [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  
   * **Balance Sheet** – snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  
   * **Break‑Even Analysis** – the point where operating expenses equal sales [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  
   * **Notes & Critical Assumptions** – explain the logic behind each number [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=20).  
8. **Exhibits** – attach supporting docs such as resumes, purchase agreements, contracts, floor plans [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Choose an Accounting Method**  
   * **Cash Method** – record income when received and expenses when paid. Suitable if you have no inventory [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
   * **Accrual Method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred. Required if you hold inventory [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
   * Small business taxpayers may treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies to use cash method [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
   * Any change in method requires IRS approval (Form 3115) [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

2. **Set Up Books & Record‑Keeping**  
   * Decide between **single‑entry** (daily cash receipts, monthly summaries) or **double‑entry** (journals and ledgers) [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  
   * Maintain a **business checking account**, record all receipts and withdrawals, and keep deposit slips, check stubs, and canceled checks as supporting documents [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  
   * Reconcile the bank statement to the checkbook each month to verify balances and spot errors [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  
   * Keep a **Petty Cash Fund** for small payments, attaching each slip to a receipt [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13).  
   * Use journal entries for all transactions (e.g., rent, supplies, payroll) and post them to ledgers [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  
   * If you use computer software, ensure it can produce legible, complete records that match your books and support your tax return [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  

3. **Inventory Accounting (if applicable)**  
   * Record inventory’s purchase price and use it to calculate Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
   * For small business taxpayers, inventory can be treated as non‑incidental materials and valued at the first use or consumption date [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

4. **Tax‑Related Set‑Up**  
   * Obtain an **EIN** if hiring employees or paying federal excise taxes [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6).  
   * Decide on a **tax year** (calendar or fiscal) when you file your first return; change requires Form 1128 [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=21).  
   * Keep a complete, separate set of records for each business if you operate multiple entities [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

5. **Reporting & Deductions**  
   * Include income and expenses in the **income statement** and **balance sheet** for each tax year [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  
   * Take **business expense deductions** (ordinary and necessary) on Schedule C or the appropriate form [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)[[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=39).  
   * Track **bad debt deductions** if you use accrual accounting and have uncollectible receivables [[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32).  

**Key Takeaway**

Combine the structured plan format outlined in Segment 1–7 with a robust accounting framework from Segment 3, 5, 6, 25, 26, and the tax‑specific guidance in Segment 20–22. This gives you a clear roadmap for drafting your business plan and a sound accounting system that supports accurate record‑keeping, financial statements, and compliance with IRS rules.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, you must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if your business meets any of the following conditions:  
* You pay wages to one or more employees.  
* You file pension or excise tax returns.  
* You are a partnership, corporation, or an LLC that is not a sole‑prop [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

A sole proprietor who has no employees can use his or her Social‑Security number (SSN) as the only taxpayer‑identification number. If you choose to use an EIN instead of an SSN for your business, that is optional but you can do so as well.  
(If the business changes form or ownership you may need a new EIN – see Segment 1, 1‑3.)

**What accounting method does an EIN “come with”?**  
An EIN does not lock you into a specific accounting method.  You can select either the cash method or the accrual method (and, if necessary, special or combination methods) when you file your first income‑tax return.  The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.  

* **Cash method** – report income when you receive it and deduct expenses when you pay them.  
* **Accrual method** – report income when earned and deduct or capitalize expenses when incurred.  If you keep inventory, the IRS generally requires the accrual method for sales and purchases [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

You must consistently use the same method for all tax filings, and changing methods typically requires IRS approval.  The accounting method you use is chosen at the time you file your first return, not by having an EIN [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

**Summary**  
* Get an EIN if you pay employees, file certain tax returns, or are a partnership/corporation/LLC—otherwise a sole proprietor may use an SSN.  
* Your accounting method is chosen separately: cash or accrual, depending on your business facts such as inventory. The presence of an EIN does not prescribe a particular accounting method.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
The injury‑record forms you must keep are the OSHA shop‑floor forms:

* **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
* **OSHA Form 301** – the Injury and Illness Incident Report (used as a supplement for each recordable event)  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – the Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses that is prepared annually  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) explains that these three forms are the core records that employers record and maintain.  

For retention, OSHA requires that these injury and illness records be kept at the worksite for a minimum of **five (5) years** after the date of the incident.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) confirms the five‑year requirement and notes that worker medical and exposure records must be retained for the period required for each specific type of record.  

So, keep Forms 300, 301 and 300A on file for at least five years (and keep associated medical/exposure documentation for whatever time the specific regulations require).

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must keep business tax records for a length of time that allows the IRS to verify and administer your return. The retention period is tied to the “period of limitations” for that tax year.  

* For ordinary income‑tax returns, keep any record that supports an item of income or deduction until the period of limitations for that return expires. The IRS generally allows you 3 years to amend a return and 3 years for the IRS to assess additional tax, so most records are kept for at least 3 years from the filing date.  
* If you are required to keep employment‑tax records, keep them for **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  
* Records relating to property (property depreciation, amortization, or basis calculations) must be kept until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property.  
* Once records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you verify that no other purpose (e.g., insurance, creditors) requires a longer retention period.  

The specific limitation periods are listed in the IRS table (Table 3) found in the publication: 3 years for most ordinary returns, 6 years for certain income‑shortage or loss situations, and “not limited” for topics such as fraudulent returns.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several essential purposes that help you run, report, and protect your business:

1. **Show your income and expenses to the IRS**  
   The IRS requires that you keep records that support the amounts reported on your business tax return. These records back up income, deductions, and credits and help you respond to any IRS inquiries.  
   – Supporting documents (receipts, invoices, etc.) must be retained so you can prove the amounts you report.  
   – You are required to keep these records for the period of limitations that applies to each tax return (typically 3‑4 years, depending on the type of item) in order to avoid penalties or difficulties if your return is examined. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

2. **Manage the day‑to‑day business**  
   Good records let you see how your business is performing—what items sell, where cash flows, and which expenses need trimming. They form the basis for financial statements (income statement, balance sheet) that help you make decisions, secure loans, or attract investors.  
   – A “good records” system is described in Segment 5, where it is said that records “monitor the progress of your business” and help you “prepare accurate financial statements.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **Support deductible expenses**  
   If you forget an expense when you file your return, you’ll lose the deduction. Keeping records of each expense as it occurs ensures you can claim all allowable deductions.  
   – Segment 3 explains that you may “forget expenses unless you record them when they occur.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **Avoid penalties and legal problems**  
   The IRS can assess penalties if you fail to keep records, or if the records you keep are incomplete or inaccessible when required. The IRS may also test your electronic storage system; if it fails, you could face additional penalties.  
   – Segment 1 notes that “you may be subject to penalties for non‑compliance” if you don’t meet storage and retention rules. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

5. **Make accurate payroll, employment taxes, and other filings**  
   Records of payroll, employment taxes, and related documents are needed to file forms such as Form 941, W‑2s, 1099s, etc. Failure to keep proper records can trigger audit issues or liability.  
   – Segments 2 and 4 reference employment‑tax recordkeeping requirements. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

In short, keeping thorough, organized, and timely business records helps you meet tax obligations, manage your business effectively, and avoid penalties or audits.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS lets you pick an accounting method when you file your first business tax return that contains a Schedule C (Form 1040). After that, you must stick with the same method unless you go through the proper change‑of‑method process (Form 3115) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

---

### 1.  Two basic methods

| Method | When income is reported | When expenses are reported |
|--------|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Cash** | When you receive the money (or when a check is cleared) | When you pay (or when a check is written) |
| **Accrual** | When you earn it (even if you haven’t been paid) | When you incur the expense, regardless of payment |

You can also use a **combination** of cash and accrual for different parts of your business, but the rules for the combination must be followed (see § "Combination Method") [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).

---

### 2.  Which one should you use?

| Situation | Preferred method | Why it works |
|-----------|------------------|--------------|
| **No inventory** and you’re operating a *small* business (average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million) | **Cash** | Easier to track; IRS allows it for most small businesses that don’t keep inventory | 
| **Inventory is required** for your business (e.g., you buy, manufacture, or hold goods for sale) | **Accrual** (unless *small business* and you elect to treat inventory as non‑incidental materials) | Accrual must show the cost of goods sold; the IRS generally requires it for inventory‑bearing businesses | 
| **Mixed inventory situation** (you keep inventory *and* have other income or expenses that are better tracked cash‑basis) | **Combination** | Use accrual for inventory and the related sales and purchases; use cash for the rest | 
| **You’re a sole proprietor with very low receipts** and no inventory | **Cash** | Easiest and most common for sole proprietors; satisfies the “small business” “cash method” exception [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Key rule:** If any inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must use accrual *unless* you meet the small‑business exemption. A small‑business taxpayer is defined as having average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million for the last three tax years (indexed for inflation) and not being a tax shelter [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). If you’re a small business, you may choose to treat inventory as “non‑incidental materials or supplies”; in that case you can still use the cash method for the rest of the business [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).

---

### 3.  How to choose the method

1. **Check your inventory status**: Do you buy, hold, or produce goods that will be sold?  
   - *Yes* → accrual (or combination).  
   - *No* → cash (if small business).

2. **Check your receipts**: Is your average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million?  
   - *Yes* → small‑business exemption applies.  
   - *No* → you must generally use accrual if you have inventory.

3. **Inventory exception check**:  
   - If you do have inventory but you can treat it as “non‑incidental materials” and you’re a small taxpayer, cash is still allowed.  

4. **File the first return** with the chosen method.  
   - If you later decide to switch, file Form 3115 and obtain the IRS’s approval. Changing the method also requires changing the treatment of any material item. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

---

### 4.  Things to remember

| Item | Important detail |
|------|-----------------|
| **Consistency** | The same method must be used for all income‑tax returns and for all books/records that support those returns. |
| **Physical inventory** | If you keep an inventory, you must record its beginning and ending balances each year and use accrual for purchases and sales unless you are a small business using the non‑incidental method. |
| **Combination limits** | If you mix methods, the combination is treated as the cash method for reporting income and expenses unless you follow the strict rules in the combination section. |
| **Change forms** | Form 3115 is required to change an accounting method after the first return. If you qualify for an automatic change, you can get approval without a fee; otherwise a ruling fee applies. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To identify hazards in your work‑site you can follow a systematic, OSHA‑recommended approach that is laid out throughout the handbook.

1. **Baseline hazard identification** – Start with a routine workplace self‑inspection.  The handbook states that a “knowledgeable and experienced worker should conduct routine safety and health inspections (self‑inspections) so the only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly”​[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklists** – The handbook includes checklists that cover general industry workplaces (except construction and maritime).  Select the checklists that fit the areas most critical to your business, then add or delete items so they match your specific processes​[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

3. **Compile and analyze the data** – Combine completed checklists with injury/illness logs, training records, maintenance logs, and incident reports.  This helps you “determine where challenges exist” and “find solutions” from OSHA standards or other resources​[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

4. **Integrate the seven core elements of a safety program** (management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, education and training, program evaluation and improvement, communication and coordination).  OSHA describes this step‑by‑step approach and emphasizes that regular inspections are key to “identifying hazards and fixing them”​[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

5. **Check specific workplace components**  
   * **Walkways and working surfaces** – Keep them clean, dry, and free of obstructions; repair holes; provide guards if elevated more than 4 ft (1.2 m); inspect regularly​[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78).  
   * **Housekeeping** – Maintain clear space in front of electrical panels; protect exits; use local exhaust ventilation where dust or fumes are produced​[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=12).  

6. **Verify compliance with applicable OSHA standards** – Review the relevant 29 CFR subpart (e.g., Subpart H for hazardous chemicals) and confirm whether the standards apply to your business.  Hazards not covered by a specific OSHA standard may be covered by the general duty clause​[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91).

7. **Use hazard communication tools** – Keep a current chemical inventory, Safety Data Sheets (SDS), and labels, and train workers on the hazards and controls​[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=38).

8. **Leverage available resources** – Contact your local OSHA On‑Site Consultation program for a no‑cost, confidential visit.  Consultants can help you “identify safety and health hazards” and advise on compliance and training​[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).

9. **Document everything** – Record safety meetings, hazard reports, training sessions, and corrective actions.  This documentation is essential for monitoring effectiveness and fulfilling OSHA paperwork requirements​[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9).

By following this process—starting with routine self‑inspections, using the handbook checklists, compiling all logs, checking specific workplace areas, verifying standards, and making use of OSHA resources—you can systematically discover and control hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting simply counts the money that actually moves in or out during the tax year.  
• Income is reported in the year you **receive** it (or constructively receive it).  
• Expenses are generally deducted in the year you **pay** them, except that certain payments made in advance are deducted only in the year to which they apply [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

Accrual‑method accounting matches income and expenses to the period in which they are earned or incurred, not when cash changes hands.  
• Income is included when the **all‑events test** has been met (the right to receive the money exists and the amount can be reasonably determined) and **economic performance** has occurred, even if you do not get paid until a later year.  
• Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, regardless of when the cash is paid, and economic performance must also have occurred [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

Key differences  
1. **Timing of income** – cash: when money is received; accrual: when earned, often before cash arrives.  
2. **Timing of expense deductions** – cash: when cash is paid; accrual: when the obligation is incurred.  
3. **Inventory rule** – if your business must keep inventory to reflect income, you are required to use the accrual method for inventory purchases and sales (small‑business exceptions apply) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  
4. **Constructive receipt** – some cash‑method taxpayers may report income before actually receiving it if it is made available without restriction (e.g., a check that could be cashed). This is treated as income for the year it’s constructively received [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

In practice, many sole proprietors and small businesses choose cash because it is simpler, but if you sell or buy inventory, or have significant receivables or payables, the accrual method is typically required or more accurate for matching revenues and costs.

1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
