runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax‑recordkeeping**

| What to keep | How long to keep it |
|--------------|---------------------|
| Copies of all filed tax returns (including Schedules, Forms 941, 940, 1099, etc.) – they help when you prepare future returns or the IRS audits you. | Until the period of limitation that applies to that return has expired. Generally the limitation is the time you can amend the return or the IRS can assess additional tax – see Table 3 in the guidance. |
| Supporting documents that prove your income and deductions, such as: sales slips, bank deposit slips, cancel‑checked checks, invoices, credit‑card charge slips, payroll records, petty‑cash slips, and asset purchase or sale documents. | As long as the related tax return could be legally challenged.  For most ordinary business items this means **the period of limitation for that return** (often 3–4 years). |
| Employment‑tax records (e.g., Forms 941, 944, wage‑books, backup‑withholding statements). | **At least 4 years** after the date the tax became due or was paid (whichever is later) – Pub. 15. |
| Asset‑related records (purchase price, improvements, depreciation schedules, disposition data). | Until the period of limitation expires for the year you dispose of the asset in a taxable disposition. |
| Records that were useful for other purposes (e.g., insurance, creditors). | Do **not** discard them until you confirm no longer needed for those purposes. |
| Electronic versions of hard‑copy books and records. | Must meet the same retention guidelines as the hard copies; keep the electronic system in place for as long as the records are material to tax administration. |


**OSHA injury & illness recordkeeping**

| Record | How long to keep it | Key reporting deadlines |
|--------|--------------------|------------------------|
| OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) and the supplementary 300A (annual summary) | **At least 5 years** at the worksite | If you have ≥100 workers in a high‑hazard industry, you must submit the 300A summary to OSHA electronically by **March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered. |
| OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | **At least 5 years** (in the same filing system as the 300 logs) | Same 5‑year retention applies. |
| Worker medical and exposure records | As long as the specific type of record requires (e.g., medical treatment records, exposure monitoring) | |
| Worker training records | Retain so they can be accessed for review | |

*Fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours (fatality) or 24 hours (other serious incidents).*

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Starting a business**

1. **Choose a legal structure** – The most common choices are a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or limited‑liability company (LLC).  The type you select determines the forms you will file and the taxes you will pay.  See the table that lists federal tax responsibilities for each structure [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2).

2. **Get a taxpayer identification number** – If you are a sole proprietor you can use your Social‑Security number as a TIN, but most businesses obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  The EIN is used on all business tax returns and for hiring employees [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2).

3. **Adopt a tax year** – You may use a calendar year (January 1–December 31) or a fiscal year that ends on the last day of a month other than December.  You will automatically use the year you first file a return unless you request a change with Form 1128.  Adopting a calendar year is required if you keep no books or you have no annual accounting period [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

4. **Pick an accounting method** – Most small businesses use the cash method (record income when received and expenses when paid).  If you keep inventory you may need the accrual method.  Once chosen, you must use the same method consistently unless you get IRS approval to change it [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

5. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – Keep business and personal finances separate.  Use the account to record every receipt and disbursement, and reconcile it monthly [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).

6. **Set up a bookkeeping system** – Use journals and ledgers (or an electronic accounting system) that clearly show gross income, deductions, and credits.  Keep supporting documents such as sales slips, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, and bank statements separate for each business if you operate multiple businesses [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

**Keeping your taxes organized**

1. **Maintain accurate records** – Your books must show a complete and separate record of every transaction.  Store paper copies or a complete electronic storage system that can index, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce the books in a legible format.  Destroy hard copies only after an electronic system has been verified to meet the IRS requirements [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

2. **Keep supporting documents** – For every expense or income entry keep a receipt, invoice, or equivalent proof.  Organize them by year and type.  Business receipts, cash registers, and bank deposit slips are typical examples [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

3. **File the correct returns** – The form you use depends on your business type (Schedule C for sole proprietors, Form 1065 for partnerships, Form 1120 for C corporations, etc.).  Also file employment forms (941/944, W‑2, W‑3) and information returns (1099‑MISC/NEC) as required [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6).

4. **Pay estimated tax when required** – If you expect to owe $1,000 or more in tax for a sole proprietor, partnership, or S‑corp shareholder, you must make quarterly estimated tax payments using Form 1040‑ES.  Corporations must pay estimated tax if they expect to owe $500 or more [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6).

5. **Pay employment and excise taxes on time** – Submit federal employment tax deposits (SSF & Medicare, FUTA, etc.) via the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS) before you file the return.  If you are subject to excise taxes (e.g., fuel, heavy trucks, wagering), file the appropriate quarterly or annual excise return and make deposits as required [

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you should track for taxes**

| What to track | Why it matters | Period & detail | Segment(s) |
|---------------|----------------|-----------------|------------|
| **Federal, state, local and foreign income taxes that are directly tied to your business** – e.g., the state gross‑income tax you pay on the business revenue (§2) | These are deductible on Schedule C (Form 1040) and reduce your taxable income (§2) | Every tax year; keep the exact tax bill or notice | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Employment‑related taxes** – Social Security, Medicare, FUTA, state unemployment, disability, and paid‑family‑leaving‑fund taxes you pay as an employer (§2) | These are deductible as business expenses (§2) | Paid monthly/quarterly per tax‑withholding schedule | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Self‑employment (SE) tax** – the 15.3 % Social Security/Medicare tax that self‑employed persons pay (§2) | Half of the SE tax is deductible on Schedule 1 (Form 1040) (§2) | Paid with quarterly estimated tax payments or at year‑end | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Personal‑property tax** – state or local taxes on personal property used in the business (§2) | Deductible as a business expense on Schedule C (§2) | Bill each tax‑year; record date & amount | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Real‑estate tax** on business property (lease‑hold, owned, or rented) (§2) | Deductible on Schedule C if the property is used for business (§2) | File the tax notice; keep the receipt | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You **do** need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) **if any of the following apply** to your business:

* You plan to hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax.  
* You are a partnership, corporation, or an LLC that is taxed as a corporation.  
* You have a sole‑proprietorship and want to use a separate TIN instead of your Social‑Security number (the IRS recommends this to keep business and personal taxes distinct).  
* You will file payroll or other employer tax returns.  

*If none of these situations fit you, a personal SSN can serve as your TIN, but obtaining an EIN is still a good idea for opening business bank accounts, credit lines, and keeping business records clean.*  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

---

### What accounting method can you use?

When you file your first business income‑tax return you choose an accounting method. The IRS does **not** tie the type of method to the EIN; you are free to select either the **cash** method **or** the **accrual** method (or a specialized combination, if the guidelines allow).  

| Method | When income is reported | When expenses are deducted |
|--------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Cash** | When you actually receive the money. | When you actually pay the money. |
| **Accrual** | When you earn the money – even if you receive it later. | When you incur the expenses – even if you pay them later. |

If you have inventory that is part of your income‑generating process, the IRS generally requires you to use the **accrual** method for inventory purchases and sales, unless you qualify as a **small‑business taxpayer** (average receipts ≤ $31 million for the past three years). Small businesses may treat certain inventory items as non‑incidental materials or supplies and can continue using the cash method for them.

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
You should keep the OSHA injury‑recording forms for every recordable injury or illness:

* **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses, used to record each incident.  
* **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report, a supplementary record for each recordable case.  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses, an annual summary of the year.  

All three forms (300, 301, and 300A) must be retained at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** after they are created.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark you must first check that the mark you want to use isn’t already in use, and then file an application with the appropriate government office.

1. **Check the status of your proposed trademark** – Search the trademark databases to be sure the name or design hasn’t already been registered.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

2. **Choose the level of protection** –  
   * **State‑level registration**: file with the Secretary of State in the state where you will do business.  
   * **Federal‑level registration**: file with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for nationwide protection.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

3. **Prepare and file your application** –  
   * For state registration, submit a trademark application (often online or by mail) to the Secretary of State’s office.  
   * For federal registration, submit a trademark application to the USPTO, which includes a search of existing marks, a description of the goods/services, and a specimen showing use.  
(Details of the filing forms and procedures can be found on the USPTO website.)  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

4. **Pay the filing fee** – Fees vary by state and by federal application type. Pay the required amount at the time of filing.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

5. **Wait for examination and approval** –  
   * The state office or the USPTO will review the application.  
   * If approved, you will receive a registration certificate and exclusive rights to use the mark in your designated class of goods or services.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**Contact information**

* Secretary of State (state‑level): (605) 773‑2797 – https://sdsos.gov/  
* USPTO (federal‑level): (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199 – https://www.uspto.gov  

That is the process outlined in the provided documents. If you need more detailed instructions or help with the application, you can contact the USPTO or your state’s Secretary of State office.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

- **General tax‑return records** – Keep the records that support any item of income or deduction *until the period of limitations for that return runs out*. The IRS generally allows you 3 years from the date you filed the return to amend it or claim a credit or refund, and the same 3‑year period for the IRS to assess additional tax. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Copies of filed returns** – Keep copies of every tax return you file; they help prepare future returns and are useful if the IRS needs to review a past return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Property (assets) records** – Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. These records are needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, depletion, and the basis for any gain or loss when the property is sold or otherwise disposed of. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Other purposes** – Once the IRS no longer needs a set of records, you may still have to keep them longer if, for example, an insurance company or a creditor requires them. Review such other‑purpose needs before discarding records. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Summary**  
- Store all records that back up income and deductions until the corresponding tax‑return period of limitations ends (usually 3 years).  
- For employment taxes, store records for 4 years.  
- For property, keep records until the limitation period for the year in which you dispose of the property ends.  

These rules are drawn directly from the IRS guidance in the provided documents.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **To monitor and manage your business** – Good records let you see whether the business is improving, which items sell best, and what changes you need to make. They also help you keep a clear picture of income and expenses. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

2. **To prepare accurate financial statements** – Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets are built from your records. These statements are useful for dealing with banks, creditors, and for internal decision‑making. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **To support the information you report on your tax return** – The IRS requires that the entries in your books be backed up by supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, etc.). Keeping these documents shows the IRS how you arrived at the amounts reported and can help avoid penalties. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

4. **To satisfy IRS record‑keeping and retention rules** –  
   * You must keep records that support any item of income or deduction until the period of limitation runs out (generally the period in which you can amend a return or the IRS can assess additional tax). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   * Employment‑tax records must be kept at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   * Records relating to assets must be kept until the period of limitation expires for the year the property is disposed of. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **To be prepared for an IRS audit or test** – The IRS may examine your books and may test your electronic storage system, requiring you to provide all records in a legible format. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

6. **To preserve evidence for other purposes** – Even after the IRS no longer needs them, you might need the records for insurance claims, creditor disputes, or other legal matters. Before discarding, verify any required retention period for those purposes. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

In short, keeping organized, accurate records lets you run your business effectively, file correct tax returns, meet legal obligations, and defend yourself if an audit occurs.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**Short answer:** Most new small‑business owners use the **cash method**, unless the business keeps inventory or is a “small business taxpayer” that must use accrual for inventory. The choice is made when you file your first tax return for the business, and once chosen you must keep the same method (or obtain IRS approval to change it with Form 3115). --- ## 1. What the IRS says | Topic | Key points from the IRS guide | |-------|-------------------------------| | **Definition of an accounting method** | A set of rules for when and how income and expenses are reported; must also be the method used to keep books. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Choices available** | • Cash method
• Accrual method
• Special methods for specific items
• Combination of the above (subject to rules) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **When you choose** | At the time you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040). To change the method later you normally need IRS approval. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Why a method must “clearly show your income”** | It must consistently use the same accounting principles that reflect revenue and expense recognition for the business. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | --- ## 2. Cash vs. Accrual | Feature | Cash Method | Accrual Method | |---------|-------------|----------------| | **When income is reported** | In the year you receive it. | In the year it is earned (receipt of payment may be later). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **When expenses are deducted** | In the year you actually pay them. | In the year the expense is incurred, whether you pay it that year or later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Inventory consideration** | If you have inventory you **must** use accrual **unless** you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer. | Needed when inventory is necessary to account for sales. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Typical applicants** | Sole proprietors, independent contractors, and small businesses with no inventory. | Manufacturers, wholesalers, and businesses with significant inventory. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | --- ## 3. When you *must* use accrual * **Inventory is required** – e.g., you produce, purchase, or sell goods that are held for sale. * **Small‑business exclusion** – Every taxpayer that is *not* a small‑business taxpayer is required to use accrual for inventory. A small‑business taxpayer has average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million over the previous three years (inflation‑adjusted) and is not a tax shelter. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | --- ## 4. When cash is generally acceptable | Criterion | What it means | Reference | |-----------|---------------|-----------| | **No inventory** | The business does not keep goods for sale, or the inventory value is negligible (less than $25,000 for most sole proprietors). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | | **Small‑business taxpayer** | Meets the $31 million gross‑receipts rule and is not a tax shelter. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | | **Tax‑year type** | You can use either calendar or fiscal year; it does not affect the choice of cash vs. accrual. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | --- ## 5. How to “change” an accounting method 1. **File Form 3115** – Application for Change in Accounting Method. You may need to pay a user fee unless you qualify for an automatic change. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) | 2. **Automatic change** – If the tax law allows, you can presume approval and apply the new method in the year you request the change. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) | 3. **Approval needed** – For most switches, you must get written consent from the IRS before applying the new method. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) | --- ## 6. Practical checklist for a newcomer 1. **Decide inventory status** * If you carry inventory: plan for accrual (unless small‑business exemption). * If you don’t: cash is usually simpler. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | 2. **Choose a tax year** – calendar (Jan 1–Dec 31) or fiscal (12‑month period ending not Dec 31). The method you pick does not depend on the tax year. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | 3. **File your first return with Form 1040/Schedule C** – include the accounting method you’re choosing. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | 4. **Keep books that match the method** – daily receipts and expenses for cash; detailed sales/inventory records for accrual. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) | 5. **Monitor IRS rules for small‑business exemptions** – keep an eye on gross receipts and adjust if you grow past the $31 million threshold. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) | 6. **If you later want to switch** – file Form 3115 and wait for IRS approval. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) | --- ### Bottom line * **If you have no inventory** or meet the small‑business inventory exemption, **choose the cash method** for simplicity. * **If you keep inventory** and are not exempt, **choose the accrual method**. * **Once chosen, stick with it** until you receive IRS approval for a change (or your circumstances change). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | **Sources:** 1. runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the practical steps outlined in the handbook:

1. **Conduct a routine self‑inspection** – Have knowledgeable and experienced workers walk through the worksite and look directly at work processes to see if hazards exist and if they are under control.  
   *Use the self‑inspection checklist in the handbook as a starting point, and adapt it to the areas most critical to your business.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the provided checklists** – These are general‑industry tools (not for construction or maritime) that list common hazards and control options.  
   *You may add or delete items so the checklist fits your specific work processes.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Compile and cross‑reference data** – Combine the completed checklist information with injury/illness records, worker training logs, maintenance logs, and incident reports. This helps spot patterns and identify remaining gaps. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Identify applicable OSHA standards** – Review the standards that apply to your business (General Industry, Construction, etc.) and analyze potential hazards in those areas.  
   *If unsure, contact your local OSHA office or state On‑Site Consultation program.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. **Establish a systematic program** – A safety and health program that includes:
   - Management leadership and commitment
   - Worker participation in identifying hazards
   - Hazard identification and assessment
   - Hazard prevention and control
   - Training and education  
   *Regular workplace inspections are a key tool for finding and fixing hazards.* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

6. **Train workers** – Ensure that employees know how to recognize hazards and that they are trained on specific controls and on reporting any new or changing hazards. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

7. **Review and improve** – After each inspection, update the hazard list, implement controls, track effectiveness, and adjust the program as needed. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

These steps provide a structured way to locate, document, and mitigate hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting are the two main ways a business can record its income and expenses for tax purposes.

**Cash method**  
* You report income only when you actually receive the money.  
* You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you actually pay them.  
* This method is simplest and is often used by small businesses that do not keep inventory.  
* Example from the text: a check received on December 30, 2025, but deposited on January 4, 2026, would be counted as income for 2026 because the cash was received in that year【Segment 18】.

**Accrual method**  
* You report income in the year you earn it, even if payment comes later.  
* Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you pay them.  
* This method matches revenues with the expenses that helped generate them, giving a clearer picture of yearly profitability.  
* The IRS requires inventory‑holding businesses to use accrual for sales and purchases, but small businesses may elect cash unless they keep inventory.  
* Example given: a computer sold on December 28, 2025, billed in January 2026 and paid in February 2026, must include the income in 2025 because the sale was earned then【Segment 1】.

**Key differences in practice**

| Aspect | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is recognized** | When cash is actually received or constructively received | When the right to receive the income is fixed and the amount can be determined accurately |
| **When expenses are deducted** | When the cash is actually paid | When the expense is incurred and all events fixing liability have occurred, and economic performance has occurred【Segment 2】 |
| **Inventory requirement** | Usually no need to keep inventory records unless the business is a small‑business taxpayer with inventory | Must keep inventory records and use accrual for purchases/sales if inventory is necessary |
| **Simple use** | Often used by sole proprietors and small businesses without inventory | Common for businesses that keep inventory or provide services over time, or that want a clear picture of profit and loss |

**When to choose each**

* If your business records no inventory and can keep numbers simple, the cash method is often easier.  
* If you have inventory, long‑term contracts, or you want to match income with the expenses that produced it, the accrual method is required or preferable【Segment 5】.

In summary: **Cash accounting records money when you touch it, while accrual accounting records economic activity when it happens, regardless of when the money changes hands**.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
**Yes — you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are incurred while you’re traveling for business.** The IRS allows you to claim most of the costs that are directly related to the business purpose of the trip, subject to the limits and rules in the cited sections. | What you can deduct | How it is measured | Key limits / requirements | |--------------------|--------------------|---------------------------| | **Transportation (to & from the business destination)** | • Air, train, bus, or car rides between your home/tax‑home and the destination;
• Taxi, limousine, or commuter‑bus fares between the airport/rail‑station and your hotel or between the hotel and a site where you work. | Must be ordinary and necessary for the business. (Seg. 2, “Transportation”) | | **Local business transportation (inside the tax‑home)** | • Mileage for driving between your home and a temporary workplace or between two regular workplaces.
• Standard mileage rate for 2025 is 70 ¢ per mile, or you may choose actual expenses (fuel, insurance, depreciation, etc.). | Standard mileage excludes car insurance, but you may still deduct parking fees and tolls. (Seg. 3, “Local business transportation” and Seg. 9, “Standard mileage rate”) | | **Rental‑car expenses** | Only the portion of the cost that is for business use. | (Seg. 1, “If you rent a car while away from home on business, you can deduct only the business‑use portion.”) | | **Airfare, train, bus, taxi, limousine, commuter‑bus fare** | Full cost. | (Seg. 2, “Transportation.”) | | **Baggage, shipping, sample or display material** | Full cost. | (Seg. 3, “Baggage and shipping.”) | | **Parking, tolls, tollways** | Full cost. | (Seg. 3, “Parking” and “tolls.”) | | **Meals** | • **50 %** of actual meal expenses (unless a special allowance applies)
• Or the standard meal allowance (Pub. 463). | 50 % limit applies to most meals. runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
The executive summary is a brief, one‑ or two‑paragraph overview that comes at the very start of the business plan. It should give the reader a snapshot of what you want to accomplish, including:

* A description of your business idea.  
* How much money you need and what it will be used for.  
* How much money you have already invested in the business (or plan to bring in).  
* A short schedule of your key goals.  

Because it is a summary, it is written last, after the rest of the plan is completed, so that it can concisely reflect the detailed information that follows.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
**How to describe your target market**

1. **Pick the niche that matters most** –  
   *Identify the group of customers who will buy your product or service first and keep coming back.*  
   * [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) tells you to “Describe your market niche; who is your best customer.”

2. **Characterise that group** –  
   • **Demographics** (age, gender, income, education)  
   • **Geographic** (city, neighbourhood, region)  
   • **Psychographics** (lifestyle, values, buying motives)  
   • **Behavioural** (purchase frequency, brand loyalty)  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) says: “Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. Consumer (household) markets might be segmented by demographics, geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought.”

3. **Estimate scope and growth** –  
   *Use public data (population figures, industry reports, sales‑tax data, etc.) to approximate how large the market is and how fast it’s growing.*  
   * [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14) continues: “Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”

---

### Quick‑start example

| What you do | Target group | Key characteristics | Size/Opportunity |
|-------------|--------------|----------------------|------------------|
| Gluten‑free muffins | Health‑conscious families (ages 25‑45) | Live in urban area, earn >$60k/year, value organic ingredients | 350 k households in city X, 10% growth per year |

*You show that you’ve narrowed the market, listed its traits, and backed it up with numbers.*

---

**In short:**  
1. Name the niche.  
2. List its demographic, geographic, psychographic and behavioural traits.  
3. Add an estimate of how many people or businesses fit those traits and what share you plan to capture.

That is the framework for describing the target market in a business plan.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) a private business that serves the public is considered a **public accommodation** and is required to remove “barriers” that are **readily achievable**.  
That means you must make your shop physically accessible to people who use wheelchairs, such as:

* **Entrance** – Provide at least a 36‑inch wide entry door (or a ramp with a slope no steeper than 1:12) and an accessible route that is level and free of steps or steep slopes. If a single entrance is not fully accessible, an alternate entrance must be available and marked with a sign that points to it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
* **Doors** – Replace round knobs or panels that need a tight grasp with lever or loop handles so the door can be opened without tight grasping, pinching, or twisting. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
* **Corridors and aisles** – Keep aisles at least 36 inches wide (42 inches preferred) and provide 30 × 48 inch clear floor space at any accessible counter or service area. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
* **Counters and service areas** – Provide an accessible counter section no higher than 36 inches and at least 60 inches long, or a lowered serving area that meets the same height and width requirements. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
* **Other barriers** – Remove steps, narrow doors, turnstiles that are too narrow, or other architectural features that block wheelchair access, unless removal is not “readily achievable.” In such cases you must offer an alternate service (e.g., staff assistance, home delivery). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)  

Because your shop serves members of the public, it is subject to these ADA obligations. If you cannot make an entrance fully accessible, you must provide an alternate accessible route or replace the barrier if it is readily achievable. Failure to comply can lead to enforcement action, legal liability, or loss of business.  

**Bottom line:** In order to comply with the ADA, you are required to make your shop wheelchair accessible—or at least make the barriers that are readily achievable removable. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

runs.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
runs.answer:

runs.question: when do i report an amputation to osha
runs.answer:
Report an amputation to OSHA within 24 hours of it occurring (or being discovered). All work‑related amputations, along with inpatient hospitalizations and loss of an eye, must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours, while fatalities require an 8‑hour report [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
Yes – you are **partially exempt** from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules if you meet certain conditions.  
- If you had **10 or fewer employees** at any time during the last calendar year, or  
- If you are in one of the low‑hazard industries listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A,  
you do **not** have to maintain OSHA Forms 300 (log) and 301 (incidence report), although you must still:  
  * report all work‑related fatalities, inpatient hospitalizations, amputations, and eye‑loss cases to OSHA, and  
  * keep records that are required for other purposes for at least five years.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
You must keep all OSHA injury‑and‑illness records—Form 300 (log), Form 301 (incident report), and the Form 300A summary—at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** from the date the record was created.  This retention period applies regardless of whether you file the summary electronically or on paper. runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax records**

| What you need to keep | How long you must keep it | Source |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|--------|
| Copies of **filed tax returns** (the return itself and any supporting schedules) | Until you can no longer be charged for that return – that is, until the period‑of‑limitations for the return expires. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| All **records that support an item of income or deduction** (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll records, depreciation worksheets, asset records) | Until the applicable period‑of‑limitations runs out (usually 3‑6 years, depending on the type of return). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (e.g., W‑2s, payroll registers, FICA and FUTA records) | At least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Asset and disposition records** (purchase/basis, improvements, sales, depreciation schedules) | Until the period‑of‑limitations expires for the year you dispose of the asset (since that determines depreciation, amortization, and gain/loss). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Any **other supporting documents** that prove the amounts reported on your returns (e.g., cash‑register tapes, deposit slips, canceled checks) | At least as long as you must keep the tax return that reports them (i.e., until the period‑of‑limitations runs out). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37) |

**Injury/illness records**

| What you must keep | How long you must keep it | Source |
|--------------------|---------------------------|--------|
| **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses), 301 (Incident Report), and 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | **At least 5 years** from the date the record was completed. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** required to confirm the details of an injury or illness | For the period specified by the type of record (e.g., the required duration for medical treatment records). | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Electronic submission of Form 300A** when applicable | Must be filed each year by **March 2** of the year following the calendar year covered, if your establishment has ≥ 250 workers, or 20‑249 workers in a high‑injury industry. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) |

**Summary**

- For tax purposes, keep every document that backs up income, deductions, and credits until the IRS period‑of‑limitations ends (usually 3‑6 years). Employment‑tax records stay for 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid. Asset records remain until the year‑of‑disposition period‑of‑limitations ends.

- For workplace injuries, keep OSHA Forms 300/301/300A and all related medical/exposure records on hand for **at least 5 years**. Submit the annual summary (Form 300A) to OSHA by March 2 of the following year if you meet the size thresholds.

These timelines are the minimum retention periods required by the IRS and OSHA; you may need to keep some records longer if another agency (e.g., an insurer or lender) asks you to do so.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Starting a business**

1. **Pick a business structure** – Decide whether you’ll operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC.  The structure determines the tax forms you’ll file and whether you need an employer‑identification number (EIN).  See the “What new business owners need to know” table and the sections on “Determining Which Type of Business to Use.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

2. **Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)** – Obtain an EIN if you have employees, operate a corporation, or want to keep your personal Social‑Security number separate.  Instructions for getting an EIN are in the “Employer Identification Number (EIN)” section. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=1)  

3. **Choose a tax year** – Most small businesses use a calendar tax year (Jan 1 – Dec 31).  If you need a fiscal year, file Form 1128 to get approval.  The choice is made when you file your first return. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Pick an accounting method** – Use the cash method (report income when received, expenses when paid) unless you keep inventory; then use the accrual method.  The method you choose must be used consistently for all tax filings. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

5. **Open a business‑only checking account** – Keep business and personal funds separate.  Deposit all receipts into the business account and write checks only for business expenses.  Record deposits and withdrawals daily. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

6. **Set up a record‑keeping system** – Combine a business checkbook, a daily cash‑receipts book, a disbursements journal, and, if you choose double‑entry bookkeeping, journals and ledgers.  Supervisory controls and a chart of accounts should be documented for electronic systems.  This maintains a complete set of books that supports your tax return. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

**Keeping your taxes organized**

1. **Reconcile your bank statements monthly** – Compare the bank statement to your checkbook and journal.  Correct any discrepancies involving bank charges, deposits after the statement date, or checks that haven’t cleared.  Reconciliation confirms you have the correct balance and records. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

2. **Keep receipts and supporting documents** – Store sales slips, invoices, cancelled checks, deposit slips, and any proof of payment.  If you pay by cash, attach a petty‑cash slip.  These documents are required to substantiate your expenses. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

3. **Track assets** – Maintain records for business property (purchase date, cost, improvement costs, depreciation, disposal details, etc.) so you can calculate depreciation or year‑end gains/losses. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

4. **File the right tax forms** – 
   * Sole proprietors: Form 1040 + Schedule C, Schedule SE, Form 1040‑ES (estimated tax) [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
   * Partnerships: Form 1065, Schedule E for partners [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
   * Corporations: Forms 1120 or 1120‑S, Form 1120‑W (estimated tax), employment tax forms 941/944 and 940 [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  

5. **Pay estimated taxes** – If you expect to owe $1,000+ in tax as a sole proprietor, partner, or S‑corp shareholder, file quarterly payments with Form 1040‑ES.  Corporations owe $500+ in estimated tax.  Deposits are made

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**How to write a business plan**

1. **Cover Page** – name, address, phone, owners’ contact, logo, date of plan.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  
2. **Table of Contents** – optional but helpful for long plans.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  
3. **Executive Summary** – a brief overview (1–2 paragraphs) that tells the reader what the business is, how much money is needed, where the money will be used, and a short schedule of goals.  Write this last.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  
4. **Business Description** – product/service overview, sustainable competitive advantage, regulations, facilities, and equipment needed.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  
5. **Management Plan** – organizational structure, owners and their ownership percentages, key staff responsibilities, day‑to‑day manager, and accounting/operations lead.  
   *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)*  
6. **Market Analysis** – total market, target market, competition, pricing, and promotion strategy.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  
7. **Money Section (Financial Projections)** –  
   * *Summary of Financial Need* – total cost, working capital, equity investment, and loan amount.  
   * *3‑Year Income Projection* – monthly projections for a 3‑year span.  
   * *Statement of Cash Flow* – cash inflow/outflow for 3 years.  
   * *Balance Sheet* – assets, liabilities, net worth as of a fixed date.  
   * *Break‑Even Analysis* – units or revenue needed to cover operating expenses.  
   All must be supported by the markets, assumptions, and notes you add.  
   *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)*  
8. **Exhibits/Appendices** – resumes, contracts, purchase agreements, floor plans, Licences, and industry reports.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*  

**How to set up accounting**

1. **Choose an accounting method** – cash or accrual (inventory cases may require accrual).  The method must “clearly show your income” and must be the same for all books and for tax filing.  If you later change method you need IRS approval via Form 1128.  
   *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)*  
2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN)** if you have employees or you prefer a tax ID.  Sole proprietors without employees may still want one.  
   *[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)*  
3. **Open a business checking account** – keep it separate from personal accounts.  Use a checkbook that records deposits (source: business, personal, loan, etc.) and writes checks payable only to business payees.  Keep deposit slips and receipts; use a daily summary cash receipts book.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)*  
4. **Record transactions every day** – use a checkbook or, preferably, a computerized system that produces machine‑sensible records.  Journal entries (double‑entry) or a single‑entry daily summary can be used.  The journal records each transaction’s date, description, debit, and credit; the ledger holds the totals by account.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*  
5. **Reconcile the checking account monthly** – compare bank statement balances to your checkbook/ledger, adjust for bank charges, deposits after the statement date, and uncleared checks.  The reconciliation confirms you have the correct balance and catches errors early.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*  
6. **Keep supporting documents** – invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, payroll records, etc.  Store them by year and type; keep them for at least 7 years (IRS period of limitation).  
   *[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)*  
7. **Use a bookkeeping system** –  
   * *Single‑entry* – simple daily cash receipts and monthly summaries.  
   * *Double‑entry* – journals and ledgers with debit/credit balances.  Software can automate both; ensure the system can produce clear, legible records and that you can generate the required financial statements (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow).  
   *[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*  
8. **Prepare financial statements** – once a year (or quarterly if needed) prepare an income statement, balance sheet, and statement of cash flows for internal use and for lenders/creditors.  These statements aid in negotiating loans and monitoring performance.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)*  

**Putting the plan and the books together**

- After gathering market data, write the plan sections as outlined above.  
- Use the plan’s “Money” section to create the financial projections and a sources‑and‑uses worksheet.  
- Build your bookkeeping system (cash or accrual, single or double entry) so that the same figures appear in the plan’s projections and in your actual books.  
- Periodically compare actual results to projections; update the plan as needed.  

**Helpful contacts**

- **SBDC** – free, confidential assistance for plan development, financial projections, and record‑keeping guidance.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you should track for taxes**

| Item | Why it matters | Source |
|------|----------------|---------|
| **Business income** – the money you receive from customers, clients, or sales. | Income must be reported on your return (Schedule C, Form 1040). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Business expenses** – any ordinary and necessary cost to run the business. | These reduce taxable profit. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Fuel taxes** – the portion of gasoline, diesel or other motor‑fuel taxes you pay. | They are included in the cost of the fuel and are not separately deductible. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Excise taxes** – such as those on specific products, vehicles or other activities. | Some can be deducted if they are ordinary and necessary expenses. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Employment taxes** – social‑security, Medicare, FUTA, state unemployment, etc. | You can deduct the employer’s share. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Personal‑property and real‑estate taxes** on business‑owned property. | Deductible where the property is used in the business. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Sales and use taxes paid** on purchases that become business inventory or capital assets. | Add to the basis or deduct as part of the expense. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Interest on a car loan** (if the vehicle is used for business). | Deductible even when using the mileage rate. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Business‑use portion of home‑related expenses** (rent, utilities, insurance, depreciation) if you qualify for a home office deduction. | These are normally deductible, subject to the gross‑income limitation. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42) |
| **Recordkeeping items** – receipts, invoices, cancelled checks, bank statements, mileage logs, and any supporting documents for all the above. | Required to substantiate every deduction. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |

**What you should track for travel expenses**

| Expense Category | What to record | How to compute the deduction | Source |
|------------------|----------------|-----------------------------|---------|
| **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, car rental, taxi, limousine, commuter bus. | Keep tickets, receipts, or a log of mileage (if using a personal car). | Deduct actual cost or use standard mileage rate (70 ¢/mile for 2025). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Local transportation** – trips between the work site and hotel, or between the hotel and a temporary workplace. | Keep receipts or mileage logs. | Actual cost or mileage rate. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Tolls and parking** | Receipts. | Deduct as part of transportation or actual expenses. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Business‑use mileage** | Log date, purpose, starting point, destination, total miles. | Multiply business miles by the mileage rate; keep separate for any non‑business travel. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Meals** | Receipts, date, who participated, and business purpose. | Deduct 50 % of the cost if the trip qualifies as overnight or long‑distant; you may use the standard allowance instead of actual costs. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Lodging** | Receipts, date, location. | Deduct the full cost if the trip is overnight or requires rest. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Cleaning (dry‑cleaning/laundry)** | Receipts. | Deduct as traveling expenses. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Telephone/communication** | Bills or logs. | Deduct the portion used for business travel. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Tips** | Receipts or ledgers. | Deduct tips paid for travel/meal related services. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Travel‑related reimbursements** | Keep records of employee reimbursements and whether they were under an accountable plan. | Deduct the reimbursed amounts appropriately. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| **Misc (e.g., local transportation, gifting during client visits)** | Receipts or detailed statements. | Include only ordinary and necessary business costs. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |

**Key record‑keeping points**

* Keep receipts, invoices, cancelled checks, electronic bank statements, and mileage logs for every item above. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
* Separate business from personal expenses; if a vehicle or expense is used 70 % for business and 30 % for personal, only the business portion is deductible. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
* For cash or petty‑cash expenses, keep a slip and attach the receipt. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13) |
* Use a journal or ledger to summarize cash receipts and disbursements for each month—this feeds into your annual summary for tax filing. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=17), [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Deadlines / Forms**

* **Travel expenses** are deductible on **Schedule C (Form 1040)** (line 28‑33) and you may need to write Form 1099‑NEC or MISC if you pay independent contractors. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41), [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
* **Excise‑tax return** (Form 720) is due quarterly if you have excise taxes to report. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
* **Standard mileage rate** changes annually; the 2025 rate is 70 ¢ per business mile. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |

---

**Bottom line**  
Track all business‑related income, ordinary and necessary expenses, and all travel‑related items listed above with receipts or logs. Keep these records organized by category and ready for the year‑end forms (Schedule C, expense worksheets, mileage logs, etc.). This will ensure you’re prepared to claim every allowable deduction and stay compliant with IRS record‑keeping requirements.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
You must keep the OSHA injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping forms and retain them for five years:

* **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
* **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report (supplementary detail on each recordable case)  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses (annual summary)

These records are required to be kept at the worksite for at least five years.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark you can do so either at the state level or at the federal level.  

**1. Decide whether to register state‑wide or federally.**  
 State registration gives you rights only within that state, while federal registration (through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) gives you nationwide protection and the exclusive right to use the mark for the goods or services listed in the application.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**2. Search the trademark databases first.**  
 Before filing, check the USPTO’s online database (TESS) and the state’s trademark database to make sure your proposed name, logo, or slogan has not already been taken.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**3. File the application.**  
 - **Federal filing:** Complete the online application on the USPTO website, pay the required filing fee, and submit any necessary specimen of the mark in use.  
 - **State filing:** File a “trademark registration” form (or “assumed business name”/“service mark” form, depending on the state’s terminology) at the Secretary of State office or through their online system, and pay the state‑specific fee.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**4. Follow up on the application.**  
 For federal filings, the USPTO will issue an examining attorney’s report. If there are any objections, you will need to respond within the time limits set in the examination notice. For state filings, the Secretary of State will publish a notice of registration or allow objections from other parties.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**5. Keep the registration active.**  
 After a federal registration, you must file maintenance documents and pay fees at the 5‑year, 10‑year, and 15‑year marks to keep the mark valid. State registrations usually require renewal every few years and payment of renewal fees.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: what health insurance plan should i buy for my staff
runs.answer:
The handbook indicates that a small‑business employer can purchase **group hospitalization and medical insurance** (i.e., a group health‑plan) for its employees. This type of coverage is eligible for the small‑employer health‑insurance‑premium tax credit (Form 8941) and is also deductible as a business expense.  
*Group hospitalization and medical insurance plans may also include long‑term‑care coverage if desired* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37).  
*Small‑employer health‑insurance‑premium credit can be claimed for the cost of such policies* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=20).  

Choosing a plan that covers hospital stays, physician visits, prescription drugs, and, if needed, long‑term care will give employees comprehensive medical benefits, help keep your workers healthier and more productive, and could reduce your tax liability.  Before deciding, compare the different provider options for coverage limits, network size, and premium cost, and check that the plan meets any state‑specific requirements your state’s OSHA‑approved plan may impose.
